setup.zh: 正殿里没有神像，只有一口空的石座，四方，四足。石座前立着测灵石，观主玄沉子坐在一旁。轮到你了。
setup.en: No statue in the main hall — only an empty stone seat, square, on four feet. Before it stands the spirit stone; the abbot Xuanchenzi sits beside it. It is your turn.

recap.zh: 测灵石测出了你的灵根；瞿老说「腿稳，心细」，观主说：收，外门。
recap.en: The spirit stone read your roots; Elder Qu said "steady legs, careful heart," and the abbot said: take them — the outer court.

zh: 正殿没有神像，只有一口空的石座。
四方，四足，大得能躺下一个人。
测灵石前，把手放上去——看它亮几种颜色。
en: No statue in the hall — only an empty stone seat.
Square, four-footed, big enough to lie in.
Before the spirit stone: lay your hand on it, and see how many colours it shows.

text.zh: 石座四只脚下各压出一个方方的深坑；座上空空的——原先该坐着一样极重的东西。
text.en: Under each of the seat's four feet the floor is pressed into a deep square pit. The seat is bare; something very heavy must once have sat on it.

text.zh: 石面光溜溜的，正中凹下去一块，是千百只手按出来的。你把手心在衣襟上擦了两擦。
text.en: The stone is worn smooth, a hollow pressed into its middle by a thousand hands. You wipe your palm twice on your coat.

text.zh: 殿门边靠着一把秃扫帚——扫石阶的那个老头也来了，站在柱子后头，谁也不看。
text.en: A worn broom leans by the hall door: the old man who sweeps the steps has come too. He stands behind a pillar and looks at no one.

story.zh:
正殿在山门里头最高的一层台子上。殿很大，很旧，梁上的彩画褪得只剩了影子，殿里没有神像，只在正中间，摆着一口空的石座。那石座四四方方，底下四只脚，大得能躺下一个人，石面正中一块颜色比别处深，四四方方，像是许多年前，那上头曾经压过一样很重很重的东西。石座前头，立着一块一人多高的测灵石，灰扑扑的，看不出什么稀奇。石座旁边一张蒲团上，坐着观主，一身灰袍，面目温和，看上去比山下镇上卖布的掌柜还要和气几分。那扫地的老头不知什么时候也进了殿，拄着扫帚，靠在门框上，身上还沾着林子里的松针。

过了三试的孩子，统共一百来个，在殿里排成长长的一队。小满上石阶走在最后，排队也排在最后，只马小宝一个是滑竿抬上来的，排在他后头。一个唱名的执事，四十来岁，生着一张没睡醒的脸，靠在柱子上。有孩子问这石座是做什么的，为什么不供神仙，他打了个呵欠，道：「每三年都有人问。」

他便讲了，讲得极熟，像是背书：「古时候，天下有九口鼎，大禹铸的。周朝的时候，鼎在周天子那里。后来周朝不行了，鼎就没了——有人说，是沉到了咱们底下这条泗水里。秦始皇统一天下，路过这里，斋戒了，祷告了，发了一千个人下水去捞。」一个孩子问：「捞着了没有？」执事道：「《史记》上就两个字：弗得。」又一个孩子问：「一千个人，捞一口锅，都捞不着？」执事看了那孩子一眼，道：「那不是锅。」顿了一顿，又道：「……好吧，也算是锅。本观开山的祖师，就在这山上结了庐，守着这条河，说鼎是有灵的，德到了，它自己会浮起来。这石座，就是给它留的——留了三百年了。」那孩子又问：「那它浮起来了没有？」执事道：「你看这上头，有鼎么？」殿里的孩子们都笑了。小满没有笑。

执事又打了个呵欠，拿下巴指一指测灵石，照例背规矩：「手按上去。石头照你身上的五行亮：金是金色，木青，水黑，火红，土黄。亮一种颜色的，单灵根，又叫天灵根，上上之资——本观三百年，没测出过一个。天灵根的孩子，还在襁褓里，便叫大宗门拿银子抱走了，轮不到泗水边上来爬台阶。亮两种，双灵根，上中；亮三种，真灵根，中上；亮四种，下中。五种都亮的——」他拖长了声音，「杂灵根，下下。颜色越少、越亮，越好。」队里有个孩子接了一句顺口溜：「杂灵根，杂货铺，样样有，样样不值钱。」殿里又是一阵笑。执事也不管，又道：「今年外门，收一百零八个。测完了，玄沉子观主点头，便是收。」他提着笔，在名册上一个一个地数，收一个，划一笔。

队伍一寸一寸地往前挪。前头每亮一回石头，殿里便响一回：亮得好的，一片惊叹；亮得暗的，一片笑。小满一面挪，一面数，像他娘拨算盘珠子：前头还有三十一个人，名册上还剩三十二个名额——够，连他，刚刚够。挪到前头剩二十个的时候，身后一挤，马家的家丁把马小宝塞到了他前头。小满又数了一遍：前头二十一个，名额二十一个。他自己，是第二十二个。昨夜廊下那个光脚的孩子也在队里，脚底板上的草叶子还没摘，一按，亮了四种颜色，「下中」。观主点了头，他咧开嘴，回头冲人堆里竖起一根指头——一两个里的一个。孙二狗排在小满前头不远，回过头来冲他咧了咧嘴，小声道：「三步一口气。」小满道：「你也上来了？」孙二狗道：「香剩最后一点点的时候上来的。」二试他是把五搁在了中间，「因为五在一到九的正当中，跟饭碗搁在桌子正当中一个道理」，老执事听了半天，说道理不对，意思对了，给他画了一道；三试他是闭着眼睛冲进去的，冲到古松底下，一头撞在树上，撞出一个包，算是摸过了。小满听得直乐，心想：这人跟我一样，都是凭自己的土法子进来的。

轮到孙二狗了。他把手放上去，测灵石半天没有动静，好一会儿，才极勉强地透出一点光来，四种颜色，淡得像是隔着一层窗户纸。唱名的执事还当是石头坏了，伸手在石头上拍了两下，那光也不见亮。执事叹了口气，念道：「金、木、火、土，四灵根，色极淡。下下之资。」殿里有人笑。孙二狗没有笑，也没有低头，只把那个比他身子还大的包袱，往背上紧了紧。那包袱里装的，是他娘给他缝的三双鞋，一双比一双大，是预备着他在山上一年一年地长个子的。观主看了他一会儿，点了点头。执事划了一笔。

排在小满前面第三个的，是阿禾。她把两根小辫子往肩后一甩，把手放上去，测灵石亮起三种颜色，青、黑、黄，亮得刺眼。执事一下子睁开了没睡醒的眼睛，念道：「木、水、土，三灵根——真灵根。中上之资。」殿里一阵惊叹。小满张了张嘴，满殿的人，到底没敢喊出声来。

轮到马小宝了。执事看了一眼名册，道：「一百零七。还剩一个。」马小宝把手往测灵石上一拍，拍得「啪」的一声，好像拍的是自家的桌子。测灵石亮了，金、红、黄三种颜色，却灰扑扑的，像蒙了一层灰。执事念道：「金、火、土，三灵根，色浊。中下之资。」他伸手要过马小宝的考牌，一看，一道，一个圈，还空着一格，眉头便皱了起来。马小宝身后那个家丁凑上前，把那封盖着县衙大印的荐书又亮了一亮。执事看看荐书，看看观主。观主没有说话。执事便提起笔来，在那空着的一格里，自己添了一道，道：「荐书在，这一格，算补过了。」又在名册上写了个字，把最后那一格划掉了：「一百零八。名额满了。后头的，不用测了。」

后头只剩小满一个。他没有走。他在心里算：不测，考牌上三道，就是三道白画；测了，就算不取，名册上也有他沈小满一行。他道：「执事，我三道画满了。我测。」执事看了看他手里的考牌，打了个呵欠，拿下巴一指：「测吧。测完了下山。」

他往前走的时候，心里那块石头又压了上来——不是名额，是眼前这块测灵石。它测的是人身上的灵气；那他胸口木牌里睡着的那个，算不算他身上的？要是这石头一亮，亮出一道银光来，亮出一条尾巴来，满殿的人都瞧见了——「藏。在你打得过所有人之前，不许让任何人知道本王。」小满的手心里，登时出了一层冷汗。他隔着衣裳，把那块木牌往怀里按了按，心里说：银月，你可千万睡沉一点。木牌凉凉的，一动不动，凉得像一块真正的木头。那不是她睡得沉，是她把自己藏起来了，藏得比他还好。

他把手放在测灵石上。
story.en:
The main hall stood on the highest terrace inside the gate. It was large and old, the paintings on its beams faded to shadows; there was no statue in it, only, in the very middle, an empty stone stand. The stand was square, four feet beneath, big enough for a man to lie on, and in the middle of its top was a patch darker than the rest, square, as if many years ago something very, very heavy had once pressed there. In front of it stood a spirit-testing stone taller than a man, dusty grey, nothing remarkable to look at. On a cushion beside the stand sat the abbot, in a grey robe, his face mild, looking even kinder than a cloth merchant in the town below. The old sweeper had come into the hall too, no one knew when, leaning on his broom in the doorway, pine needles from the forest still on him.

The children who had passed all three trials, a hundred or so in all, lined up in a long queue in the hall. Xiaoman had climbed last and queued last; only Ma Xiaobao, carried up by chair, stood behind him. A name-calling steward of about forty, with a face that had never quite woken up, leaned on a pillar. A child asked what the stand was for, and why there were no gods; he yawned. "Every three years someone asks."

So he told it, fluently, as if reciting: "In ancient times there were nine *ding* under heaven, cast by Yu the Great. In the Zhou dynasty the *ding* were with the Son of Heaven. Later the Zhou declined, and the *ding* were lost — some say they sank into this very Si River below us. When the First Emperor of Qin unified the world he passed through here, fasted, prayed, and sent a thousand men into the water to dredge for them." A child asked: "Did they find them?" The steward said, "The *Records of the Grand Historian* give it two words: not found." Another asked: "A thousand men dredging for one pot, and they couldn't find it?" The steward gave that child a look. "It isn't a pot." A pause. "…All right, it's a sort of pot. The founder of this temple built a hut on this mountain to watch over the river, and said the *ding* had a spirit: when virtue arrived, it would float up of itself. This stand was left for it — left three hundred years." The child asked again: "Has it floated up?" The steward said, "See a *ding* up there?" The children in the hall all laughed. Xiaoman didn't.

The steward yawned again, pointed his chin at the testing stone, and recited the rules as usual: "Hand on it. The stone lights by the five elements in you: metal gold, wood green, water black, fire red, earth yellow. One colour: a single root, also called a heavenly root, the highest of the high — this temple hasn't tested one in three hundred years. Heavenly-root children are carried off in swaddling clothes by the great sects, for silver; they never get as far as climbing stairs by the Si. Two colours, a double root, above the middle; three, a true root, just above the middle; four, below the middle. All five lit —" he drew it out, "— a mixed root, the lowest of the low. The fewer the colours and the brighter, the better." Someone in the queue chimed in with a jingle: "Mixed root, mixed-goods shop — a bit of all, and none worth a copper." Another laugh round the hall. The steward ignored it. "This year the outer court takes a hundred and eight. When you're tested and Abbot Xuanchenzi nods, you're in." Brush in hand, he counted down the register one by one, a stroke for each taken.

The queue crept forward inch by inch. Each time the stone lit up front, the hall made a noise: a bright one, a gasp; a dim one, a laugh. Xiaoman counted as he shuffled, like his mother at the abacus: thirty-one people ahead, thirty-two places left in the register — enough; counting himself, just enough. When the ones ahead were down to twenty, there was a shove from behind: the Ma servant had squeezed Ma Xiaobao in ahead of him. Xiaoman counted again: twenty-one ahead, twenty-one places. He himself was the twenty-second. The barefoot boy from last night's veranda was in the queue too, grass leaves still under his soles; he pressed, and four colours lit — "below the middle". The abbot nodded, and the boy grinned and held up one finger to the crowd behind him — one of the one or two. Sun Ergou, not far ahead, turned round and grinned, and said softly: "Three steps a breath." Xiaoman said, "You made it up too?" Sun Ergou said, "Came up when there was just a tiny bit of incense left." In the second trial he'd put the five in the middle, "because five's right in the middle of one to nine, same as you put the rice bowl in the middle of the table"; the old steward had listened a long while, said the reason was wrong but the idea was right, and given him a stroke; in the third he'd charged in with his eyes shut, run head first into the old pine, raised a bump, and that counted as touching it. Xiaoman listened grinning, thinking: this one's like me — got in on his own home-made ways.

Sun Ergou's turn. He laid his hand on it, and for a long while the stone did nothing; then, very grudgingly, a little light seeped out, four colours, faint as if seen through window paper. The name-calling steward thought the stone had broken and slapped it twice; the light got no brighter. The steward sighed and read: "Metal, wood, fire, earth, four roots, very faint. The lowest of the low." Someone in the hall laughed. Sun Ergou didn't laugh, and didn't lower his head either; he only hitched the bundle bigger than himself higher on his back. In it were three pairs of shoes his mother had sewn, each bigger than the last, for him to grow into year by year on the mountain. The abbot looked at him a while, and nodded. The steward made a stroke.

Third in line ahead of Xiaoman was Ahe. She flicked her two little braids back over her shoulders, laid her hand on it, and the stone lit three colours, green, black, yellow, dazzling. The steward's sleepy eyes flew open. "Wood, water, earth — three roots — a true root. Just above the middle." A gasp went round the hall. Xiaoman opened his mouth — with the whole hall there, he didn't dare call out after all.

Ma Xiaobao's turn. The steward glanced at the register. "A hundred and seven. One left." Ma Xiaobao slapped his hand on the stone with a smack, as if slapping his own table at home. The stone lit gold, red and yellow, but dull and grey, as if filmed with dust. The steward read: "Metal, fire, earth, three roots, muddy. Below the middle." He held out his hand for Ma Xiaobao's tag, looked — one stroke, one circle, one space empty — and frowned. The servant behind Ma Xiaobao stepped up and showed the letter with the county seal once more. The steward looked at the letter, looked at the abbot. The abbot said nothing. So the steward lifted his brush and drew a stroke in the empty space himself. "There's a letter; this space counts as made up." He wrote a word in the register and struck out the last place. "A hundred and eight. The places are full. The rest needn't be tested."

Only Xiaoman was left behind. He didn't go. He reckoned: not tested, three strokes on his tag were three strokes for nothing; tested, even if not taken, the register would have a line with Shen Xiaoman on it. He said: "Steward, my three strokes are full. I'll be tested." The steward looked at the tag in his hand, yawned, and pointed his chin. "Go on then. Then go down the mountain."

As he walked up, the stone on his mind pressed down again — not the places: this testing stone before him. It tested the spirit in a person; did the one asleep in the token at his chest count as in him? If this stone lit up and showed a streak of silver, a tail, with the whole hall watching — "Hide. Until you can beat everyone, no one may know about this king." Xiaoman's palms broke out in a cold sweat. Through his clothes he pressed the token tighter to his chest, and said in his heart: Yinyue, sleep sound, please. The token was cool and still, cool as a real piece of wood. It wasn't that she slept sound. She had hidden herself — hidden better than he had.

He laid his hand on the stone.

label.en: Give your birthday · The root test

exits.means: gives the day they were born, or lets the stone read them — the page card asks it

story.zh:
测灵石亮了——亮得很暗。

金、青、黑、红、黄，五种颜色，一样不少，都有一点，哪一种都不多，哪一种都不亮，你挤着我，我挨着你，灰蒙蒙地搅在一处，像他娘拿家里用剩下的五种碎布头，拼成的一块抹布。{主亮}

殿里静了一静。

然后，有人笑出了声。笑得最响的，是马小宝。他笑得前仰后合，笑得手里的桂花糕渣子掉了一地，拿手指着那块测灵石，像是指着一个天大的笑话。他这一笑，殿里的孩子们便都笑了，一个传一个，一片一片地笑开去，笑声撞在那褪了色的大梁上，又落下来。

唱名的执事也笑了一笑，拖长了声音念道：「金、木、水、火、土——五行俱全。五行杂灵根。下下之资。」他提起笔来，「名额已满。不取。」

笔尖朝名册上「不取」那一栏落下去。小满站在测灵石跟前，手还放在石头上，没有拿下来。三百级是他自己走上来的，洛书是他自己算出来的，蠪侄的真头是他自己听出来的——到头来，一块石头，一支笔。他想起舅舅在一百六十级上坐下的那一炷香，想起他娘在老槐树底下停在半空的那只手。满殿的人，笑的笑，看的看，只有两个人没有笑：一个是蒲团上的观主；另一个是阿禾。她站在人堆后头，低着头，拿炭条在本子上记了一笔，记得很重，炭条都记断了。

小满在心里飞快地算了一笔账：不说，是出去；说了，最多也是出去。他把手从测灵石上拿下来，从怀里摸出那块考牌，举了起来，道：「执事。」殿里的笑声小了一些。他道：「今天早上，石阶顶上那位老人家说，沉鼎观收人，不看出身，不看荐书，只看三样：腿，脑子，胆子。」他把考牌翻过来，让执事看那三道，「三样，我这牌子上画满了。」他顿了一顿，没有看马小宝，只道，「最后那个名额，牌子上一个圈，一道是执事自己添的。」

殿里一下子静了。静了一会儿，队伍前头，孙二狗一声不吭，也把自己的考牌举了起来。跟着，那个光脚的孩子也举了起来，举得高高的，牌子上三道，是他一试一试爬出来的。举牌子的只有这两个，别人都低着头。

执事的脸涨成了猪肝色，笔尖一转，指着小满喝道：「放肆！名额的事，轮得到你一个杂灵根来说？来人——」

笔尖离名册还有一寸，观主开了口：「慢。」他看了看测灵石，又看了看小满。他看小满的时候，比看测灵石的时候长得多，长得小满都有点发毛了。然后他转过头去，问靠在殿门口的那个人：「三试。瞿老以为如何？」

殿里的孩子们这才知道，那扫地的老头，原来是有名字的。瞿老拄着扫帚，只说了四个字：「腿稳。心细。」殿柱边上的几个老执事，互相看了一眼。瞿老在沉鼎观扫了五十年的台阶，四十多年没有收过一个徒弟；这四十多年里，他评孩子的话，统共评过不到三回，每回不超过两个字。

玄沉子点了点头：「收。外门。」执事的笔停在半空，道：「观主，名额——」玄沉子道：「添一个。」

执事张了张嘴，到底没说出什么来，低下头，在名册的末尾添了一行，又在那一行后头，添了两个小字：顶撞。然后挨个收新弟子的考牌。收到小满跟前，门口的瞿老道：「留着。」执事的手缩了回去。马小宝从小满身边走过去的时候，瞿老拿扫帚把门槛扫了一下，扫得很响。马小宝压低了声音，道：「沈小满，杂灵根也配进山门？等着。在这山里，我有的是法子收拾你。」小满道：「小宝哥，裤子干了吗？」马小宝张嘴要骂，一口桂花糕呛进了气嗓，咳得满脸通红，一个字也没咳出来。

那天夜里，有个起夜的老弟子路过正殿，看见观主一个人坐在那口空石座旁边的蒲团上，也不打坐，也不念经，看着那口石座，一直坐到了三更。
story.en:
The spirit-testing stone lit — very dimly.

Metal, green, black, red, yellow — five colours, not one missing, a little of each, none much, none bright, jostling one another, stirred together grey and murky, like a rag his mother had stitched from five kinds of leftover scraps. {主亮}

The hall went still for a moment.

Then someone laughed out loud. Loudest of all was Ma Xiaobao. He laughed till he rocked, laughed cake crumbs all over the floor, pointing at the testing stone as if at the joke of the century. With him laughing, the children in the hall all laughed, one catching it from the next, spreading patch by patch, the laughter hitting the faded beams and falling back down.

The name-calling steward smiled too, and drew it out as he read: "Metal, wood, water, fire, earth — all five elements. A mixed five-element root. The lowest of the low." He lifted his brush. "The places are full. Not taken."

The brush tip went down toward the "not taken" column of the register. Xiaoman stood before the testing stone, his hand still on it, not taking it away. Three hundred steps he had walked himself, the Luo Shu he had reckoned himself, the Longzhi's real head he had heard himself — and in the end, a stone and a brush. He thought of his uncle sitting down on step one hundred and sixty for a stick of incense; of his mother's hand under the old locust, stopped in mid-air. The whole hall was laughing or looking, and only two did not laugh: the abbot on his cushion, and Ahe. She stood at the back of the crowd, head down, and made a note in her book with the charcoal, so hard the charcoal snapped.

Xiaoman ran a quick sum in his head: say nothing, and he's out; speak, and at worst he's out. He took his hand off the testing stone, took the trial tag from his jacket, and held it up. "Steward." The laughter in the hall thinned. He said: "This morning, the old man at the top of the stair said Chending Temple takes disciples not by birth, not by letters of recommendation, but by three things only: legs, head, nerve." He turned the tag so the steward could see the three strokes. "Three things — my tag's full." He paused, didn't look at Ma Xiaobao, and said only: "The last place — its tag has a circle on it, and one stroke the steward drew himself."

The hall went silent at once. After a moment, near the front of the line, Sun Ergou, without a word, held up his own tag. Then the barefoot boy held his up too, high, three strokes on it, climbed one trial at a time. Only those two raised their tags; everyone else kept their heads down.

The steward's face went liver-red; he swung the brush tip round at Xiaoman and barked: "Insolence! Are the places the business of a mixed root? Someone —"

The brush tip an inch from the register, the abbot spoke: "Wait." He looked at the testing stone, then at Xiaoman. He looked at Xiaoman much longer than at the stone, so long Xiaoman's skin began to prickle. Then he turned and asked the man leaning in the doorway: "The three trials. What does Elder Qu think?"

Only then did the children in the hall learn that the old sweeper had a name. Elder Qu leaned on his broom and said just four words: "Steady legs. Careful heart." A few old stewards by the pillars exchanged a look. Elder Qu had swept the temple's stair for fifty years and taken no disciple in over forty; in those forty-odd years he had given a verdict on a child fewer than three times, never more than two words a time.

Xuanchenzi nodded. "Accepted. Outer court." The steward's brush hung in mid-air. "Abbot — the places —" Xuanchenzi said: "Add one."

The steward opened his mouth, said nothing in the end, lowered his head and added a line at the end of the register — and after that line, two small characters: *insubordinate*. Then he went along collecting the new disciples' trial tags. When he reached Xiaoman, Elder Qu in the doorway said: "Keep it." The steward's hand drew back. As Ma Xiaobao walked past Xiaoman, Elder Qu swept the threshold once with his broom, very loud. Ma Xiaobao said under his breath: "Shen Xiaoman, a mixed root, fit for the gate? You wait. On this mountain I've ways enough to deal with you." Xiaoman said, "Xiaobao-ge, are your trousers dry yet?" Ma Xiaobao opened his mouth to curse, choked on a mouthful of osmanthus cake, and coughed till his face went scarlet without coughing out a single word.

That night an old disciple, up in the night, passed the main hall and saw the abbot sitting alone on the cushion beside the empty stone stand, not meditating, not chanting, looking at the stand, until the third watch.
